retention audit preview · klaviyo · australia + us

The drops do most of the selling, but the flows underneath them are currently leaking strong revenue levers.

We went through both Klaviyo accounts flow by flow. This is what we found, in the order we'd fix it, and what we think it's worth.

Every revenue figure in this document is shown as a range. This is just a contextual estimate, sized from each account's own numbers, not a forecast.

8 + 8core flows to rework, eight in each account, on top of the new ones
A$1.6M–3.0M+ US$1.3M–2.5Ma year in revenue we can see room for (an estimate)
3channels run as one journey: email, SMS and app push
12touchpoints reach Klaviyo with no flow attached

01 · the short version

CSB already has the hard part: people want what it makes.

Drops sell out. A million people follow the brand on Instagram. Members-only launches are the best-performing emails in both accounts. The demand is there. What hasn't kept up is the Klaviyo set-up underneath it, which was built for a store that sells the same catalogue all year and has drifted since. Here's the story in five parts, and the rest of this document walks through each one.

01 · the repair

The flows closest to a sale have the wrong rules

Some rules let the wrong people in, others keep the right ones out, and a send setting skips shoppers who've just asked for a message.

02 · the first screen

Half the flow emails make people scroll to find a button

A photo fills the screen and the offer comes after it. Most people never scroll that far.

03 · the rework

Every core flow was built for a generic store

None of them know that CSB sells in drops, or that sizes and stock run out.

04 · the gaps

12 touchpoints reach Klaviyo with nothing attached

Points about to expire, a saved item running low, a price drop. Customers are telling us what they want and getting no reply.

05 · the biggest one

The pop-up converts 2–4% of visitors, and a million Instagram followers have no way into Klaviyo.

If we only did one thing, it would be this. At an 8% sign-up rate we estimate it's worth A$700k–1.3M and US$350k–650k a year, before counting what the celebrity collabs could add.

02 · the repair

We'd start with the flows that run when someone is closest to buying.

Every flow has a set of rules that decide who gets each message. We read them line by line across all 75 live flows, and the same few mistakes kept coming up.

1Who hears from us first

When someone leaves a cart today, Klaviyo picks one channel for the first message based on what they once signed up to. If they have the app, they get a push and nothing else. That's half of AU cart shoppers, on the channel that earns the least.

Sending every shopper an email first, then adding SMS and push by channel preference, is worth an estimated A$180k–320k and US$100k–200k a year.

2Rules that let the wrong people in, and keep the right ones out

This is the cart flow's rule as it's set up today. Joining exclusions with OR means meeting any one of them is enough, so someone who has already started checkout still qualifies for the cart email. We found the same kind of slip in seven other places.

the rule today
what it should read
Profile filtersEdit
Checkout Started zero times since starting this flow
AND
Checkout Started - Instant Audiences zero times
AND
Cart viewed / checkout started - IA zero times
AND
Placed Order zero times since starting this flow
Each exclusion on its own row. The duplicate goes.

With "OR", passing any one line is enough. These need "AND".

FlowWhat's happeningThe fix

US browse abandonment (both)The same OR mistake, so browse emails reach people already in a cart flowAND each line

3Smart Sending, where the shopper asked for the message

Smart Sending is a Klaviyo setting that skips anyone who was messaged in the last 16 hours. It makes sense for nudges people didn't ask for. In flows the shopper set off themselves, it quietly drops the message they're waiting for, because CSB sends a campaign on about half of all days. We'd switch it off in these:

03 · the first screen

Even when the right email arrives, it makes people work to act on it.

Opening a flow email is the moment of highest intent. Someone left a cart, joined the list or just bought, and they're giving us a few seconds. Most people decide from what they see before scrolling. If a photo fills that screen and the button sits below it, the click is gone.

04 · the welcome

The welcome is where this costs the most.

The welcome was rebuilt in September. Since then it earns about a third less from every new subscriber: AU went from A$17 to A$12, the US from US$14 to US$10.

Three things changed at once. The new flow sends fewer messages and stops on day 5, even though the code is good for 14. The SMS welcome used to reach every new SMS subscriber and earned A$12–18 a text; now it only reaches people who join the email list at the same moment. And the code still sits below the first screen. In the US, the minimum spend on the code also rose from US$70 to US$99.

Before SeptemberNowA strong welcome
Emails5 over 20 days3 over 5 days5–6 over 14 days
SMSEvery SMS sign-up, A$12–18 a textOnly people joining the email list, about half as many2–3 texts, code first
Code reminderNoneNone. The code lasts 14 days; the flow ends on day 548 hours before it expires
Code on the first screenNoNoYes

Nothing in the flow checks whether someone is actually new, either. That's how 204,000 welcome messages went out on 09/11, two weeks before Black Friday, mostly to people who were already subscribed.

Getting the welcome back to where it was before September is worth an estimated A$350k–650k and US$320k–580k a year.

Welcome revenue by order month divided by new email subscribers that month, so adding or removing emails can't flatter the number.

05 · the rework

Fixing the rules gets the flows back to what they were. It doesn't make them right for CSB.

Most brands sell the same catalogue all year. CSB sells in drops, so demand comes in waves, sizes go fast and stock runs out. Not one of the core flows uses any of that. Each one needs reworking, not only repairing.

FlowWhat it's built for todayWhat it needs to do for CSB

Two gaps run through all of them. Reviews aren't connected to Klaviyo in either account, so a shopper who's unsure about a product never sees what other customers said about it, which is usually what tips them over. And customers with three or more orders have no winback at all, even though in AU the 13% of customers with ten or more orders hold 52% of customer value.

part two

Build the flows around the drop.

Everything so far fixes what's there. This part is about growing it, and it starts with how people join the list in the first place.

07 · the front door

The biggest lever is how people join, and it's barely being used.

The pop-ups were seen 2.5 million times in the last six months. Most convert at 2–4%. Meanwhile CSB's strongest channel, Instagram, has no route into Klaviyo at all.

1A pop-up built with Alia

We'd rebuild the pop-up in Alia. The Alia pop-ups we've deployed for other brands have reached about a 10% opt-in rate. The hook is a mystery discount on the first order: people sign up to find out what they've won, which converts far better than a flat 10% everyone has already seen. Early access to the next drop sits alongside it, and the phone number is asked for on a second step, once they're already in.

3The celebrity moments, in every flow

CSB's feed already has the kind of content most brands pay a fortune for. Madison Beer in the Fade Athena Tank. Hailey Bieber training in the Noa Crop and Foldover Flares. At an 8% sign-up rate, the pop-ups alone would add about 165,000 AU and 100,000 US subscribers a year. We estimate that at A$700k–1.3M and US$350k–650k.

08 · the drop

Members-first already outsells everything else. Every drop could work that way.

Early-access sends are the best-earning campaign type in both accounts. The US EOSE launch went to its waitlist first and made US$4.16 per recipient, twelve times a normal launch email. Right now that only happens when someone builds it by hand.

waitlistComing Soon pages, Instagram, the pop-up
teaserThe date and the colours
members firstEarly access for Rewards members
launchThe waitlist, then everyone
sold outBack-in-stock sign-up, plus what's left
afterComplete the set from the same drop

A waitlist flow would run this for every drop automatically. Today, people browsing Coming Soon pages are filtered out of browse abandonment and nothing else picks them up, which means the most interested visitors on the site hear nothing until launch day.

09 · loyalty

Loyalty works. Most customers just can't see their balance.

Reward Received earns A$5.43 per email in AU and US$8.70 in the US, more than almost any other flow. And yet the points balance sits near the top of just 11 of 213 AU flow emails.

A balance someone can see is a balance they spend. We'd put it in a banner at the top of every email, flows and campaigns, with the live balance and tier.

Points also expire without a word. 57,405 AU and 42,314 US members had points expiring last quarter, and none of them got a message. The same goes for members about to lose a tier.

The US needs one more step first: only 38% of US customers are Rewards members, against 68% in AU, so post-purchase should invite every non-member to join.

10 · the programme

A cashback programme with three tiers, and a club worth being in.

CSB Rewards already has the hard part: 68% of AU customers are members, and the reward emails are among the best earners in both accounts. What holds it back is the currency and the perks. A balance of 1,240 points means nothing until someone works it out, points run out without a word, and Levels 1 to 3 list almost the same benefits. We'd turn it into a cashback programme with three tiers, where every level gives more cash back and unlocks things money can't buy.

1What other brands are doing

How it worksWhat CSB can take from it

Mecca Beauty LoopNo points to count. Spend over 12 months sets your level, and each level gets a set number of gifts a year.Rewards members can see coming.
Alo AccessPoints only decide your tier. The perks are access: early drops, member-only sales, the Alo Wellness Club app.Status paid in access costs almost no margin.

lululemon membershipFree to join. Early access, member events and run clubs, free hemming.Membership feels like being let in, in person.

2What she's actually joining for

CSB's customer is a young woman who trains, shops in drops and follows the brand for the people in it as much as the product. Four things keep someone like her in a programme, and today's version only really offers the first.

money she can see

Cash back, in dollars

The strongest reason to join and stay. A dollar balance is real in a way points never are, and it pulls her back to spend it.

being first

Getting in before it sells out

Drops sell out in hours. Early access and a held size are the perks she'll talk about, and they cost CSB nothing.

belonging

Doing it with other people

Run clubs and pilates socials are how women her age meet people now. A brand that hosts them becomes part of her week, not just her wardrobe.

being seen

Being part of the brand

Voting on colourways, seeing samples first, being featured on @csb. Recognition is what turns a regular customer into someone who recommends CSB.

4The CSB Club and the member hub

The social part is what makes this CSB's own. Front Row and Inner Circle members get invites to the CSB Club: monthly pilates, run and walk sessions in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and the Gold Coast, and in LA and New York for the US. Each invite has room for a friend, which makes every event a referral.

Inner Circle members also get one big night a year, invites to launch parties, and a say in what comes next: samples to see first and votes on new colourways. The best member posts get featured on @csb, next to the celebrity collabs.

All of it lives in one place in the CSB app and on the site: the cash balance, how far she is from the next tier, when she gets into the next drop, and which Club sessions are coming up.

11 · the channel

Klaviyo already knows which channel each customer prefers. Nothing uses it yet.

For every profile, Klaviyo predicts which channel that person is most likely to respond to. That prediction should decide two things: the order of messages inside a flow, and who gets which channel when a campaign goes out.

Klaviyo channel affinitypredicted for every profile
SMS firstAU 25% · US 12%

In flows: SMS opens the journey.
In campaigns: drop launches by SMS, email as backup.

Email firstAU 11% · US 34%

In flows: email leads, SMS only on drop day.
In campaigns: email only, so fewer texts to pay for.

Not enough data yetAU 64% · US 54%

In flows: email first, push for app users.
In campaigns: every click and reply sharpens the prediction.

Share of a 6,000-customer sample in each account.

The two accounts lean opposite ways. AU customers lean towards SMS and US customers towards email, yet the flows in both route by sign-up instead. That's a good example of why the two accounts can't simply be copies of each other.

12 · why au needs its own build

Copying the US flows into AU would send the wrong message to the account's best customers.

AU and US customers buy the same product but behave differently, and the content around them is different too. These are the parts of every AU flow that have to be written and built for Australia.

What's specific to AUWhat it means for the flows
ChannelAU customers lean towards SMS: 25% rank it first, against 11% for emailTest SMS as the first touch in AU flows, where the US leads with email
The app1,001 orders came through the app since 01/11, double the USPush and app-only moments get a bigger role in AU
Loyalty68% of AU customers are Rewards membersAU flows lead with the balance and tier; the US version has to ask people to join first
Who matters mostCustomers with 10+ orders hold 52% of AU customer valueVIP lapse, early access and tier warnings carry more weight than in the US
Orders that aren't purchasesLoop exchanges (413) and Lefty gifting (253) since 01/11Excluded from every AU customer flow; the US has its own list, with Shop app, TikTok and draft orders
Prices and offersFree shipping over A$150, a A$99 welcome minimum, tier spend in A$Every threshold, banner and code line written in A$ for AU spend levels
Seasons and calendarDecember is summer; Boxing Day, Click Frenzy and EOFY in JuneProduct focus, imagery and timing follow the Australian year, not the US one
WordsAustralian spelling and phrasing, local delivery timesCopy written for AU, not converted from US English

Most of the structure can be shared. What the customer actually reads and is offered has to be AU's own, or the flows end up talking to a US shopper in an Australian inbox.

Channel affinity from a 6,000-customer predictive sample per account. Order sources since 01/11/2026. Shipping thresholds from the live AU and US storefronts.

13 · the plan

November stops the leaks. December looks after the new customers. Then we rebuild the rest.

The order follows the calendar as much as the money. Black Friday brings in more first-time customers and new subscribers than any other month, so the flows that catch them come first. And every month has two halves: what we build, and the strategy and consulting that runs alongside it from the first week.

novNovember: the repairs, then the flows that pay back fastest

We start by auditing every live flow and fixing what's leaking: the flow filters, the send settings and deliverability. That isn't about new revenue. It stops the flows sending the wrong message to the wrong people. Then the welcome, and four new flows built on urgency, where a customer is about to lose something or miss out.

decDecember: the customers Black Friday brings in

Post-purchase is the top priority. Black Friday and Cyber Monday bring a wave of first-time customers, and they need a nurture journey running behind them that turns one order into a habit. Alongside it, we rebuild abandoned cart and checkout, and add the browse journeys that catch people earlier.

febFebruary: the loyalty programme

pencilled in · if CSB goes ahead with the revamp

CSB Cash, three tiers and the CSB Club

February is set aside for the full programme from section 10. It's the biggest single piece of work in the plan, so it gets the month.

  • The programmeTiers, cash rates and rules set up, with CSB Cash issued as store credit through Rise.
  • Drop accessEarly-access windows by tier and size holds for Inner Circle.
  • The switch-overEvery points balance converted to CSB Cash, every member moved to their new tier, and one launch campaign to announce it.
  • The flowsJoin, cash landed, cash about to lapse, tier up, tier at risk, drop access by tier, birthday cash and bring a friend.
  • The CSB ClubInvites, RSVPs with a plus-one, reminders and post-event follow-ups.
  • The member hubBalance, tier progress, next drop and Club sessions in the app and on the rewards page.

If CSB keeps the current programme, February goes to its flows instead: points earned, redemption and the tier journeys.

allStrategy and consulting: from November, and ongoing

This is as much of the work as the build, and once the flows are rebuilt it becomes the core of it. Every month, we'd guide everything that runs through Klaviyo, in both accounts, not just the flows we touch.

flows

How the flows fit together

Which flow catches whom, in what order, on which channel, so no customer gets three messages in an hour or none at all.

campaigns + content

The drop calendar

Teaser, members-first and launch sends planned around each drop and Instagram post, segmented by channel preference and tier.

loyalty

The programme

Designing the revamp with the CSB team, then running the Club calendar and reading what the tiers do to repeat purchase.

account health

Deliverability and reporting

Inbox placement, list hygiene, sign-up rates and a monthly read of what's actually earning, per account.

testThen a testing workflow, once the flows are built

When a flow is rebuilt, it goes into a testing cycle: one change at a time, with the biggest flows keeping a small holdout group so we can show the real lift, not just attributed revenue.

welcome

The welcome offer

The mystery discount against CSB Cash against early access, and the US minimum spend.

abandonment

Abandonment offers

No offer, a code, or CSB Cash, and when it appears: the first message, the second or not at all.

gift with purchase

Gifts with purchase

Specific gifts against a discount, especially around drops and spend thresholds.

loyalty

The cash rate

How much CSB Cash per tier, how long it lasts, and double-cash days against straight discounts.

Every revenue range here is just a contextual estimate: Klaviyo-attributed, sized from each flow's own numbers in each account, and not a forecast. The total also counts points earned, which runs inside the loyalty flows. Price drop is sized on wishlisted items only. The loyalty revamp, site abandonment and the second-order flows are sized once there's data to size them on. Exchanges are AU only, where Loop runs.
